meta.title: Who really said "The greatest enemy of knowledge is not ignorance. It is the illusion of knowledge"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Stephen Hawking. The historian Daniel J. Boorstin wrote it — and the familiar wording is a misquotation of what he actually said.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The greatest enemy of knowledge is not ignorance. It is the illusion of knowledge'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed to Hawking only from 2001, with no evidence he ever said it. The line is Daniel J. Boorstin’s, and the popular version misquotes him.

answer.label: Not Stephen Hawking — actually Daniel J. Boorstin
answer.authorDates: 1914–2004 · American historian; twelfth Librarian of Congress
answer.sourceLine: The thought and the phrasing are Boorstin’s, from The Discoverers (1983) and a January 1984 Washington Post interview. Even so, the sentence as people quote it is not quite his: Boorstin wrote of the greatest obstacle to discovery, not the greatest enemy of knowledge. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the Hawking ascription only from 2001 and no evidence Hawking ever used the line.

source.excerpt: The greatest obstacle to discovery is not ignorance—it is the illusion of knowledge.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying to Daniel J. Boorstin and states plainly that it “has been unable to find substantive evidence that he actually employed it” of Hawking. Its earliest Hawking ascription is a “Daily Almanac” filler column in The Daily Ardmoreite of Ardmore, Oklahoma, dated 6 August 2001.

QI dates the phrasing to Boorstin’s The Discoverers (1983), which contains a version particularised to geography, and to a Washington Post interview of 29 January 1984 that carries the general form QI calls the most quotable.

Wikiquote’s Boorstin entry ↗ reaches the same conclusion independently, and goes further: it prints our exact popular wording and labels it a misquotation, noting it is “often misattributed to Stephen Hawking”.

Wikiquote’s Hawking page ↗ lists the line in its Misattributed section, crediting Boorstin. Boorstin himself did not claim the idea: QI records him calling it an aphorism, and elsewhere crediting a similar thought to Edward Gibbon.
source.excerptNote: Boorstin’s wording in the January 1984 Washington Post interview, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. The familiar version swaps “obstacle to discovery” for “enemy of knowledge”.

author.heading: About Daniel J. Boorstin
author.metaLine: 1914–2004 · American historian & twelfth Librarian of Congress
author.bio: Daniel J. Boorstin was an American historian who taught at the University of Chicago and wrote widely on American and world history. Appointed the twelfth Librarian of the United States Congress in 1975, he served until 1987 and was instrumental in creating the Library’s Center for the Book. His best-known works include The Discoverers, The Creators and The Image.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two things went wrong on the way to the version you have seen. The line was moved to a more famous name, and the words themselves were smoothed into something Boorstin never wrote.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the ascription no earlier than 6 August 2001, in a newspaper filler column, and reports no direct evidence Hawking ever used the saying. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed.
Boorstin’s documented sentence is about the greatest obstacle to discovery. Wikiquote ↗ prints the popular form verbatim and calls it a misquotation.
Historian and twelfth Librarian of Congress ↗. He used several versions across The Discoverers (1983), Hidden History (1987) and Cleopatra’s Nose (1994).

QI notes a thematically related adage in Buckle’s History of Civilization in England: “the great enemy of knowledge is not error, but inertness.” QI presents it as a precursor in theme, not as the source Boorstin was reworking.

misattribution.truthLine: The insight is Boorstin’s, the polish is anonymous, and the famous name on it is a late addition with nothing behind it ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Boorstin spent his career on discovery — how people found out about the world, and what stopped them. His point was not that ignorance is harmless but that it is honest: someone who knows they do not know will go and look. It is the confident, wrong picture that keeps you at home.

That is why the misquotation is a little sad. “The greatest obstacle to discovery” names the cost precisely: the discovery you never make. “The greatest enemy of knowledge” is a broader, blunter claim, and it loses the thing Boorstin was actually pointing at.
detailsBody: In The Discoverers Boorstin applies the idea to mapmaking: the shape of the earth and its oceans was obscured less by blank spaces than by confident, wrong charts. Imagination, as he put it, draws in bold strokes while knowledge advances by slow increments.

He was careful about ownership. Quote Investigator records that he called the notion an aphorism rather than his own coinage, and in Hidden History (1987) credited a similar thought to Edward Gibbon — that for Gibbon the menace to understanding was not so much ignorance as the illusion of knowledge.

The drift to Hawking follows a familiar rule: a saying about science migrates to the most famous living scientist. QI dates that migration to 2001, by which point the line had been circulating in Boorstin’s name for the better part of two decades.
context.pull: Ignorance sends you looking. A false picture keeps you at home.
